sections.name: MCQ Set A
tips: Read the attribution line first: who wrote it, when, and why. A Tokugawa decree, an ambassador and a modern historian each have a different purpose.
Find the main idea of each paragraph before you look at the choices. Many questions ask about one paragraph only.

For "best used as evidence of" or "best illustrates" questions, first name the bigger development the source shows (gunpowder expansion, loyal elites, legitimacy, revenue, religious change), then pick the choice that matches it.
The wrong choices are usually true-but-not-in-the-source, from the wrong empire or century, or too extreme. Cross them out with the X button.
"Practice passage" sources were written for this kit from your class materials. They are not real quotations, so don't quote them on the test.

A1.title: The fall of Constantinople, 1453
A1.attr: Practice passage in the voice of an Ottoman court chronicler writing soon after 1453.
A1.label: Practice passage written from your class materials (textbook, study guide, slides); not a real quotation.
paras: Our sultan, Mehmed, son of Murad, lay before the city of the Romans. Its triple walls had turned back army after army, and the emperor of the Romans trusted in them. But the sultan had ordered cannons cast larger than any seen before, and day and night their stones struck the walls. Where the walls fell, the Janissaries of the sultan's household rushed in, and the empire of the Romans came to its end.

When the city was taken, the sultan rode to the great church of the Romans and ordered that it become a mosque, so that the call to prayer would sound where the bells had rung. He did not leave the city empty. He made it his own capital and filled its markets on the strait between the two seas, and the Christians and Jews who lived there were allowed to keep their own communities under their own leaders.
Thus the city became the seat of the sultan, and from it his armies and his ships could reach both the lands of the Franks and the lands of the Arabs.

A2.title: The sultan's servants
A2.attr: Practice passage written in the style of a modern historian of the Ottoman Empire.
A2.label: Practice passage written from your class materials (textbook, study guide, slides); not a real quotation.
paras: The Ottoman sultans faced a problem common to rulers of large empires: the great landholding families of the provinces had their own followers and their own interests. The sultans' answer was the devshirme, a levy that took boys, usually between the ages of 8 and 20, from Christian villages in the Balkans. The boys were converted to Islam and given a demanding education in politics, the arts and warfare.

The most able were trained as scribes, tax collectors and governors; many others became Janissaries, the elite infantry who carried firearms. Although they were legally the sultan's slaves, some rose to the highest offices in the empire, positions closed to most freeborn subjects.

Because they had been cut off from their families and had no ties to local nobles, these men owed their positions to the sultan alone. In this sense the devshirme was less a form of punishment than a tool of state building, one that turned outsiders into the empire's most dependable servants.

A3.title: Outsiders on the dragon throne
A3.attr: Practice passage written in the style of a modern historian of Qing China.
A3.label: Practice passage written from your class materials (textbook, study guide, slides); not a real quotation.
paras: When rebels seized Beijing in 1644, the Manchus of the northeast saw their chance. Already organized by Nurhaci into military units called banners, they allied with a Ming general, took the capital and proclaimed a new dynasty, the Qing. Yet conquest created a new problem. The Manchus were a small minority ruling a vast Han Chinese population that had long seen northern peoples as outsiders.

The Qing emperors answered with a careful mix of adaptation and control. They kept the Confucian civil service examinations, claimed the Mandate of Heaven, and commissioned portraits showing the emperor as a model of Confucian virtue. Important offices were shared between Manchu and Han officials.

At the same time, the Manchus did not disappear into Chinese society. Han men were required to wear the queue, the Manchu hairstyle, as a sign of loyalty, and the banners remained a separate Manchu military force. Under emperors such as Kangxi and Qianlong, this combination held together a vast and growing empire.

A4.title: Taxes and the military in the Islamic empires
A4.label: Adapted from a table in your textbook (AMSCO).
table: Taxes on non-Muslims; taxes on peasants
Taxation policies used to encourage adherence to Shi'a Islam
Taxes on unbelievers abolished by Akbar but reinstated later; taxes on peasants
Warriors (often trained Janissaries) granted villages; strong navy
Qizilbash warriors helped establish the empire; no significant navy

A5.title: Beyond the Urals
A5.attr: Practice passage in the voice of a Russian official reporting to Moscow in the early 1600s.
A5.label: Practice passage written from your class materials (textbook, study guide, slides); not a real quotation.
paras: Since the great tsar Ivan took the khanates of Kazan and Astrakhan from the heirs of the Horde, the whole length of the Volga has been ours. Our merchants now sail it down to the Caspian Sea and trade with the Persians and the Turks without paying any khan for the right.

Beyond the stone mountains, the merchant family of the Stroganovs hired bands of Cossacks to go into Siberia. The native peoples there have few or no firearms; the Cossacks carry them, and so a small band can hold a whole river valley. Wherever they go they require the local peoples to pay tribute in furs, which bring great profit in Moscow.
If the sovereign continues to send men and powder, there is no river in that land that cannot be brought under his hand, as far as the sea at the eastern edge of the world.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes a claim made in the first paragraph?
options: The city surrendered peacefully after the emperor negotiated with the sultan
The sultan won mainly because his navy blockaded the strait between the two seas
Cannons broke the city's long-trusted walls, letting the Janissaries in
The Janissaries dug tunnels under the walls that the Byzantine defenders could not detect
questions.exp: Paragraph 1: giant cannons struck the walls, and where they fell the Janissaries attacked.
why: The passage describes cannons breaking the walls and Janissaries rushing in.
The navy is never credited; the cannons are.
There is nothing about tunnels; the walls fell to cannon fire.

questions.stem: The second paragraph can best be used as evidence that the Ottomans
options: forced every Christian and Jew in the city to convert to Islam
made Istanbul a trading capital where non-Muslims kept their communities
planned to abandon the city once its treasures had been carried away
feared that the Byzantine Empire would soon recover and take the city back from them
questions.exp: He made the city his capital, filled its markets, and let Christians and Jews keep their own communities: an early form of the millet system.
why: The passage says Christians and Jews kept their own communities.
He repopulated it and made it his seat.
Nothing in the paragraph suggests fear of a Byzantine return.

questions.stem: The development described in the passage most directly contributed to which of the following?
options: The Ottoman rise as a power linking Europe and Southwest Asia
The end of Ottoman expansion, since the empire now focused only on holding the city
The spread of Shi'a Islam across Anatolia and the Balkans
A lasting alliance between the Ottomans and the Christian states of Europe
questions.exp: Istanbul controlled the Bosporus, and from it the Ottomans could reach both Europe and the Arab lands, as the last paragraph says.
why: Ottoman expansion continued for another century, under Selim I and Suleiman.
The Ottomans were Sunni; the Shi'a state was the Safavids.
The Ottomans went on to fight European states, for example at Vienna.

questions.stem: Which of the following best states the historian's argument?
options: The devshirme was mainly a punishment for Christian villages that resisted Ottoman rule
The devshirme weakened the sultan by giving power to provincial landholding families
The devshirme built servants who were loyal to the sultan alone
The devshirme failed because few of the boys ever rose above the rank of soldier
questions.exp: Final paragraph: cut off from family and local nobles, they owed everything to the sultan.
why: The historian says it was less a punishment than a tool of state building.
It was designed to balance those families.
The historian says some rose to the highest offices.

questions.stem: Which evidence does the historian use to support the claim that the system offered some upward mobility?
options: The boys were taken from Christian villages in the Balkans
Some recruits rose to the empire's highest offices
The boys were usually between the ages of 8 and 20 when taken
Janissaries were elite infantry who carried firearms
questions.exp: Rising from a Balkan village to the highest offices is the upward-mobility evidence (paragraph 2).
why: Where they came from does not show that they rose.
Their age does not show advancement.
This describes their role, not a rise in status.

questions.stem: The purpose of the system described in the passage was most similar to the purpose of
options: the Safavid shahs' use of enslaved ghulams to offset the Qizilbash
the Mughal zamindars, who collected land taxes and kept a share for themselves
the Mexica practice of human sacrifice to show that the ruler pleased the gods
Luther's Ninety-Five Theses, which challenged the authority of the Catholic Church
questions.exp: Both the devshirme and the ghulams created servants who depended on the ruler alone.
why: Zamindars were a revenue system, not a loyal military elite.
That was about religious legitimacy.
That was a religious protest, not a way to build loyal officials.

questions.stem: Which of the following best states the main argument of the passage?
options: The Qing gave up Manchu customs completely and became indistinguishable from the Ming
The Qing ruled by adopting Chinese traditions while keeping Manchu ones
The Qing ruled only by military force and ignored Confucian traditions
The Qing failed to win acceptance and lost power soon after the death of Kangxi
questions.exp: Adaptation (exams, Mandate, shared offices) plus control (queue, banners).
why: The third paragraph says the Manchus did not disappear into Chinese society.
The second paragraph lists the exams, the Mandate of Heaven and Confucian portraits.
The passage says the combination held the empire together under Kangxi and Qianlong.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the Qing policies in the second paragraph developed most directly because
options: the Ming general who helped them demanded that Confucian traditions be preserved
the banner armies had been defeated and could no longer control China
Han Chinese officials refused to wear the queue until the exams were restored
the Manchus were a small minority seen as outsiders by the Han
questions.exp: The end of paragraph 1 states the problem: a small minority ruling a vast population that saw them as outsiders.
why: The passage does not say the general made any demands.
The banners remained a separate Manchu force.
The passage does not link the queue to the exams.

questions.stem: The Qing requirement that Han men wear the queue is most similar to which of the following?
options: Akbar's abolition of the jizya, which removed a burden from his Hindu subjects
The Peace of Augsburg, which let German princes choose the faith of their lands
The Safavid use of the title shah, the Persian word for king
Tokugawa alternate attendance, a visible test of the lords' loyalty
questions.exp: Both were visible demands that showed and enforced loyalty to the ruling group.
why: That was tolerance, not a required sign of loyalty.
That gave rulers a choice; it did not demand a loyalty sign.
A title is not a demand placed on subjects.

questions.stem: Which of the following conclusions is best supported by the table?
options: All three empires had strong navies that matched their land armies
All three empires taxed non-Muslims at the same rate throughout the period
The empires used similar tools but with different priorities
The Safavid Empire relied on the same Janissary system as the Ottomans
questions.exp: Same tools (taxes, warriors), different uses: Safavid taxes pushed Shi'a Islam, and only the Ottomans had a strong navy.
why: Only the Ottomans had a strong navy; the Safavids had none to speak of.
The Mughal column shows the tax abolished and later brought back.
The Safavid row lists Qizilbash warriors, not Janissaries.

questions.stem: The Mughal entry under "Taxes" best illustrates which of the following?
options: A change from Akbar's tolerance to stricter rule under his successors
A continuity in Mughal policy, since the tax on unbelievers never changed
Mughal efforts to spread Shi'a Islam through the tax system
The Mughal adoption of Ottoman tax farming in South Asia
questions.exp: Abolished by Akbar, reinstated later (by Aurangzeb): a change in religious policy.
why: The table says it was abolished and then reinstated.
That describes the Safavids, not the Mughals.
The table does not mention tax farming.

questions.stem: The expansion described in the passage was made possible most directly by
options: Ivan IV's conquests and firearms used against peoples without them
an alliance between the tsar and the Qing emperor to divide Central Asia
the Russian navy's control of the Pacific coast
Peter the Great's westernization of the Russian army
questions.exp: Paragraph 1 credits Ivan's conquests; paragraph 2 says the Cossacks' firearms let a small band control peoples without them.
why: No alliance is mentioned; the Cossacks acted for Moscow.
The passage describes Cossacks moving overland, not a navy.
Peter ruled later; this report is from the early 1600s.

questions.stem: The passage can best be used as evidence that Russian expansion in this period was driven partly by
options: religious motives, especially spreading Orthodox Christianity to Siberia
the need to escape Mongol rule, which still controlled Moscow
rivalry with the Ottomans for control of Siberia
economic motives such as trade routes and furs
questions.exp: Volga trade with Persia and the Turks, and furs that "bring great profit in Moscow."
why: Religion is never mentioned.
The passage says Russia had already taken the Horde's lands.
The Ottomans appear only as trading partners.

sections.name: MCQ Set B
tips: Read the attribution line first: who wrote it, when, and why. A Tokugawa decree, an ambassador and a modern historian each have a different purpose.
Find the main idea of each paragraph before you look at the choices. Many questions ask about one paragraph only.

For "best used as evidence of" or "best illustrates" questions, first name the bigger development the source shows (gunpowder expansion, loyal elites, legitimacy, revenue, religious change), then pick the choice that matches it.
The wrong choices are usually true-but-not-in-the-source, from the wrong empire or century, or too extreme. Cross them out with the X button.
"Practice passage" sources were written for this kit from your class materials. They are not real quotations, so don't quote them on the test.

B1.title: Rules for the great lords
B1.attr: Practice passage in the voice of a Tokugawa shogunate decree to the daimyo, early 1600s.
B1.label: Practice passage written from your class materials (textbook, study guide, slides); not a real quotation.
paras: The lords of the provinces shall come to Edo and serve the shogun in alternate years, so that each lord keeps a house in Edo and a house in his own domain. When a lord returns to his domain, his wife and children shall remain in Edo. Any lord who fails to come at the appointed time shall be judged disloyal, and his domain may be taken from him.

The samurai of each domain shall no longer live by the sword alone. They shall serve as officials of local government and receive a fixed salary, keeping the peace and seeing that what is owed is collected.
The teaching of the Christians is forbidden throughout the realm, and dealings with foreigners shall be strictly limited, so that no outside power may stir up the domains against the shogun.

B2.title: Kings above the law?
B2.attr: Practice passage written in the style of a modern historian of early modern Europe. The quotation from James I is as printed in your textbook (AMSCO 3.2).
B2.label: Practice passage written from your class materials (textbook, study guide, slides); not a real quotation.
paras: King James I of England put it plainly: "The state of monarchy is the supremest thing upon earth: for kings are not only God's lieutenants upon earth, and sit upon God's throne, but even by God himself they are called gods." Across Europe, monarchs used this idea of divine right to claim that resisting the king meant resisting God.

In France the idea reached its height under Louis XIV, who is said to have declared, "I am the state." He sent royal officials called intendants into the provinces to carry out his orders and collect taxes, and he built the palace of Versailles, where the great nobles were expected to live under his eye.

England followed a different path. After decades of conflict between kings and Parliament, the Bill of Rights of 1689 required Parliament's agreement for taxes and a standing army and guaranteed legal process before arrest. By 1700, the two kingdoms that had both been ruled by divine-right monarchs had moved in opposite directions.

B3.title: A preacher in Wittenberg
B3.attr: Practice passage in the voice of a German townsman writing in the 1520s.
B3.label: Practice passage written from your class materials (textbook, study guide, slides); not a real quotation.
paras: When I was young, the preachers came to our town selling letters of indulgence. They said that a coin in the box would shorten a soul's time of punishment, and many poor people gave what they could not spare. Bishops' offices, too, were bought and sold, and no one dared to speak against it.

Then Doctor Martin, a monk of Wittenberg, posted his theses against these practices. He taught that a person is made right with God by faith alone, not by payments or by works, and that the Scriptures stand above the word of the pope. The pope cast him out of the Church, but his words spread from town to town, and many of my neighbors came to agree with him.
Now our church is no longer the pope's. Our neighbors in the next territory still hear the Mass in Latin, and each prince decides which faith his lands will follow.

B4.title: A new faith in Punjab
B4.attr: Practice passage written in the style of a modern historian of South Asia.
B4.label: Practice passage written from your class materials (textbook, study guide, slides); not a real quotation.
paras: In the late 1400s, Punjab was a meeting ground of Hindu and Muslim communities. There a teacher named Guru Nanak began to preach that there is one God and that people are equal before God, whatever their caste. His followers, the Sikhs, became a community open to people of every background.

At first the new community grew under Mughal tolerance. Akbar granted it land, and in 1604 Guru Arjan installed the first edition of the Sikh scripture, the Adi Granth, in the Golden Temple. But under Akbar's successors relations soured. In 1606 the emperor Jahangir had Guru Arjan imprisoned and executed.

The Sikhs responded by organizing to defend themselves. In 1699 Guru Gobind Singh founded the Khalsa, a community of initiated Sikhs committed to protecting their faith. A movement that began as a message of unity had become, by necessity, an armed community.

B5.title: Sources of legitimacy
B5.label: Adapted from a table in your textbook (AMSCO).
table: Rulers in Islamic empires used the title "caliph"; European monarchs claimed divine right; Songhai rulers converted to Islam; the Aztecs (Mexica) used human sacrifice
Portraits of Qing emperors; miniature paintings in the Ottoman Empire; financial support of artists by European rulers
Mausolea such as the Taj Mahal and mosques in the Mughal Empire; European palaces such as Versailles and El Escorial

questions.stem: The rules in the first paragraph were most likely intended to
options: encourage the lords to expand their domains by conquering neighboring provinces
allow the lords to elect a new shogun every other year
convert the lords and their families to Christianity
keep regional lords watched and unable to challenge the shogun
questions.exp: Living in Edo every other year, with families left there as hostages, kept the daimyo watched and unable to rebel.
why: The rules restrain the lords; disloyal lords could lose their domains.
Alternate years refers to living in Edo, not elections.
The third paragraph bans Christianity.

questions.stem: The second paragraph best illustrates which change in Japanese society under the Tokugawa?
options: Samurai were replaced by a standing army of Janissaries recruited from abroad
Samurai went from warriors to salaried officials
Samurai lost all their status and became ordinary merchants
Samurai gained the right to choose which lord they would serve
questions.exp: "No longer live by the sword alone... serve as officials... receive a fixed salary" = swords to salaries.
why: Janissaries were Ottoman.
The decree makes them officials, not merchants.
The decree assigns them fixed duties; it does not give them choices.

questions.stem: The Tokugawa policies described in the passage are most similar to which of the following?
options: The English Bill of Rights, which required Parliament's consent for taxes
Louis XIV keeping the great nobles at Versailles
Akbar's tolerance toward Hindu subjects
The Ottoman millet system, which let religious communities run their own affairs
questions.exp: Both rulers kept powerful nobles close to the center so they could not build independent power.
why: That limited the ruler; the Tokugawa rules limited the lords.
Tolerance is the opposite of the Tokugawa ban on Christianity.
The decree bans a religion rather than letting it govern itself.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the historian's argument in the passage as a whole?
options: France and England both moved toward limited monarchy by 1700
Divine right was a uniquely English idea that France rejected
Two divine-right kingdoms ended up with very different monarchies
Louis XIV and James I agreed that Parliament should approve all taxes
questions.exp: Last sentence: two divine-right kingdoms moved in opposite directions.
why: France moved toward absolutism under Louis XIV.
The passage says the idea reached its height in France.
That was the 1689 Bill of Rights, after James I's time.

questions.stem: Which evidence does the historian use to support the claim that Louis XIV was an absolute ruler?
options: He signed the Bill of Rights to share power with an assembly
He described kings as God's lieutenants who sit upon God's throne
He used intendants and kept nobles at his palace
He allowed provincial nobles to collect taxes without royal officials
questions.exp: Intendants (central control of the provinces) and Versailles (control of the nobles).
why: That was England, and it limited the crown.
Those are James I's words, not evidence about Louis.
Intendants were royal officials sent to oversee taxes.

questions.stem: James I's claim in the first paragraph is most similar to which of the following?
options: The Chinese idea of the Mandate of Heaven
The Sikh teaching that all people are equal before God
The English Bill of Rights' limits on the monarch's power to tax
Luther's argument that the Scriptures stand above the pope
questions.exp: Both divine right and the Mandate of Heaven tie the ruler's power to a divine source. (Difference: the Mandate could be lost.)
why: That is about equality, not royal power.
That limits kings; James I exalts them.
That challenges authority rather than supporting a king's.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes a claim the author makes in the first paragraph?
options: Indulgences were freely given to the poor by the bishops
The pope had already banned the sale of church offices
Most townspeople openly protested against indulgences before Luther
Church practices took money from the poor and sold offices
questions.exp: Paragraph 1 describes indulgences sold to the poor and simony (buying and selling offices).
why: The author says preachers sold them and the poor paid.
The author says no one dared to speak against it.
He says no one dared to speak out.

questions.stem: According to the second paragraph, Luther's teaching challenged the practices in the first paragraph mainly because he held that
options: God has already chosen who will be saved, so the Church's sacraments are useless
only priests should be allowed to read and explain the Scriptures
people are saved by faith, so salvation cannot be bought with payments
the pope alone could forgive sins in exchange for good works
questions.exp: Faith alone (sola fide): if salvation comes through faith, indulgences cannot buy it.
why: Predestination was Calvin's teaching, and the passage does not mention it.
He put the Scriptures above the pope; he did not limit them to priests.
Luther rejected both payments and works as the way to be saved.

questions.stem: The situation in the last paragraph most directly reflects which of the following?
options: The Edict of Nantes, which protected French Calvinists
The Peace of Westphalia's end of all religious differences in Europe
The Anglican Church, which Henry VIII founded independent of the pope
A settlement letting each German ruler choose the faith
questions.exp: "Each prince decides which faith his lands will follow" = the Peace of Augsburg (1555).
why: That was France, and it was a royal edict, not a choice for princes.
Westphalia added Calvinism as a choice; it did not end differences.
That was England.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the change in the Sikh community traced in the passage?
options: It turned from a message of unity to armed self-defense
It moved from armed resistance toward full acceptance by the Mughal emperors
It gave up its rejection of caste in order to win Mughal support
It merged with Akbar's Din-i Ilahi and stopped being a separate faith
questions.exp: Last sentence: a message of unity became, by necessity, an armed community.
why: The order is reversed: tolerance came first, then persecution.
The passage says nothing about giving up equality.
Sikhism stayed separate and grew.

questions.stem: According to the passage, which development most directly led to the founding of the Khalsa?
options: Akbar's grant of land to the Sikh community
Mughal persecution, including Guru Arjan's execution
The installation of the Adi Granth in the Golden Temple
Contact between Hindus and Muslims in Punjab
questions.exp: After Jahangir executed Guru Arjan, the Sikhs organized to defend themselves; the Khalsa followed.
why: That was a sign of tolerance, before relations soured.
That came during the peaceful period.
That explains Sikhism's origins, not the Khalsa.

questions.stem: The table best supports which of the following conclusions?
options: Rulers in many regions used similar tools to claim legitimacy
Only Islamic empires used religion to support their rulers' authority
European rulers relied on architecture but never on religion
Monumental architecture was found only in South Asia
questions.exp: Each row mixes regions: legitimacy tools were shared across the world, in local forms.
why: Divine right and Mexica sacrifice are on the same row.
The table lists divine right under religion.
Versailles and El Escorial are European.

questions.stem: A historian could best use the "Religion" row of the table as evidence that
options: many states tied a ruler's power to divine approval
all of these rulers followed the same religion
religion weakened rulers by giving power to the clergy
rulers stopped building monuments once they claimed religious authority
questions.exp: Caliph, divine right, Songhai Islam, Mexica sacrifice: different religions, same use.
why: They range from Muslim caliphs to Christian kings to the Mexica.
The row shows religion supporting rulers.
The architecture row shows they did both.

sections.name: MCQ Set C: Class practice questions
tips: These are the 9 questions from your class's Unit 3 practice handout. The stems and passages are the handout's; the choices are reordered.
The handout came without an answer key. These answers come from the passages and AMSCO 3.1–3.4. Check them against your class's key (VERIFY).

For "best used as evidence of" or "best illustrates" questions, first name the idea the source shows (expansion, legitimacy, administration, revenue, belief systems, continuity or change), then pick the option that matches it.
Eliminate options that are true in history but not shown by the source, or that belong to the wrong time, region or empire.
Watch for extreme words ("only," "all," "never," "completely"): they are usually wrong.

C1.title: A Catholic priest meets Shah Abbas I
C1.attr: Father Simon, a European Roman Catholic priest, in a report to the pope on meeting the Safavid Shah Abbas I, 1588. From your class's Unit 3 practice questions.
C1.text: He is very valiant and has a great liking for warfare and weapons of war, which he has constantly in his hands: we have been eye-witnesses of this because, whenever we were with him, he was adjusting his [swords], testing his [muskets], etc . . . This is the great experience, which he has obtained of warfare over so many years, that he makes it in person and from the first has made him a fine soldier and very skilled, and his men so dexterous that they are little behind our men in Europe. He has introduced into his militia the use of and esteem for [muskets], in which they are very practiced. Therefore it is that his realm has been so much extended on all sides. . . . All the above mentioned soldiers, who will total some 100,000, receive pay for the whole year.

C2.title: Sunni Ali and the Songhai state
C2.attr: J. Rotondo-McCord, "Kingdoms of the Medieval Sudan," Xavier University. From your class's Unit 3 practice questions.
C2.text: Demonized as an enemy of the faith by the Muslim narrative sources, yet lionized as a warrior hero in the oral tradition, Sunni Ali, who reigned from 1464 to 1492, is one of the most controversial figures of the African Middle Ages. . . . Relying on a swift and mobile cavalry force as well as on naval control of the Niger River, Sunni Ali had conquered the agriculturally rich central Niger or 'inland delta,' including the wealthy and scholarly cities of Timbuktu and Jenne, by the 1470s. . . . He was well aware that a vast empire could not be held together by military conquests alone, but need[ed] an effective and efficient administrative structure as well. Indeed, the organization of Songhay [Songhai] government which was developed to a great degree under Sunni Ali differed substantially from previous Sudanic patterns of empire. These had been based more on alliances and relationships with tributary states than on the high degree of centralization characteristic of Songhay [Songhai].

C3.title: The Safavids and the Ottomans
C3.attr: William H. McNeill, The Rise of the West, 1963. From your class's Unit 3 practice questions.
C3.text: Throughout the sixteenth century, the Safavi [Safavid] empire remained a profoundly disturbing force in the Moslem [Muslim] world, dedicated to the defense and propagation of Shi'a doctrines at home and abroad. This policy implied a normal state of hostility with the Ottoman empire, punctuated only briefly by periods of peace. By the seventeenth century, however, when the Safavi empire reached its apogee [peak] under Shah Abbas the Great (1587–1629), the fanaticism of the Shi'a revolution had faded, at least in court circles; and a lasting peace with the Ottomans was concluded in 1639.

questions.stem: Which claim about Father Simon's purpose for meeting Shah Abbas I is best supported by the above passage?
options: Simon was impressed by the new technology used by the Safavids.
Simon wanted the pope to know of the Safavids' military power.
Simon hoped the pope would sell new weapons to the Safavids.
Simon thought the Safavids could teach Europeans about how to organize a military.
questions.exp: The report to the pope stresses the shah's skill, 100,000 paid soldiers, muskets and an empire "extended on all sides": it is a briefing on Safavid military power.
why: He mentions muskets, but the report is about the size, skill and pay of the whole army, not a new invention.
Nothing in the report asks for or offers weapons; the Safavids already have muskets.
He says the Safavid soldiers are "little behind our men in Europe": close to Europe, not ahead of it.

questions.stem: Which most strongly contributed to the historical development reflected in Father Simon's description of the Safavid military structure?
options: The Mughal emperors' support for the Sikh religion
Ottoman development of shariah
Safavid intolerance for the Sunni population
The Thirty Years' War
questions.exp: The Shi'a Safavids forced conversion on Sunnis and fought the Sunni Ottomans over religion and territory, so they built a large gunpowder army.
why: Mughal emperors did not support Sikhism; Jahangir executed Guru Arjan in 1606, and it has nothing to do with the Safavid army.
Islamic law did not cause a Safavid military build-up.
That was a European war (1618–1648), decades after this 1588 report.

g1a.title: Guns and empires
g1a.attr: Practice passage written in the style of a modern historian.
g1a.label: Practice passage written only from your teacher's Unit 3 study guide; not a real quotation.
paras: Between 1450 and 1750, the Ottoman, Safavid, Mughal, Manchu (Qing) and Russian empires grew across connected stretches of land. Historians often group the first three as "gunpowder empires," because cannons and firearms, and not cavalry alone, made their rapid growth possible.

The clearest example came in 1453. Mehmed II used massive cannons to break through the walls of Constantinople, a city that had protected the Byzantine Empire for centuries. Its fall ended that empire and handed the Ottomans one of the great trade centers of the world.

Gunpowder did not make the Ottomans unstoppable, however. In 1529 their siege of Vienna failed, and that city marked the farthest point of their push into Central Europe. Weapons explained much of the empires' growth, but political and religious rivalries also shaped where they expanded and where they stopped.

g1b.title: Rivals in faith and land
g1b.attr: Practice passage written in the style of a modern historian.
g1b.label: Practice passage written only from your teacher's Unit 3 study guide; not a real quotation.
paras: In 1514 the Ottomans met the Safavids at Chaldiran. Ottoman artillery and Janissaries defeated the Safavid army, and the victory stopped Safavid expansion to the west. Because the Ottomans were Sunni and the Safavids were Shi'a, the battle also set up a long-running Sunni–Shi'a rivalry between the two states.
The Safavids had a second rival to the east. They and the Mughals fought again and again over territory, and the religious difference between Shi'a Safavids and Sunni Mughals sharpened the conflict.

The Mughals themselves owed their empire to gunpowder. Babur founded it after winning at Panipat in 1526 with artillery. His grandson Akbar expanded it across northern India, and Aurangzeb later pushed it to its largest size in the south.

paras: Gunpowder expansion was not only an Islamic or Eurasian story. In 1591 Morocco defeated the West African empire of Songhai using firearms, showing that the same weapons could reshape states across the Sahara.

In East Asia, the Manchus overthrew the Ming dynasty in 1644 and founded the Qing. They then expanded into Central and East Asia through both conquest and alliances, including long campaigns against the Zunghars, a Mongol group in Central Asia.

Russia grew in the opposite direction. In the 1550s Ivan IV, known as the Terrible, conquered Kazan and Astrakhan, opening the way east. Cossacks armed with firearms then pushed Russian control across Siberia, where the peoples of the steppe could not match their weapons.

g2a.title: Holding an empire together
g2a.attr: Practice passage written in the style of a modern historian.
g2a.label: Practice passage written only from your teacher's Unit 3 study guide; not a real quotation.
paras: Military force alone could not hold a large empire together. Rulers also needed loyal officials, professional armies, a way to show their right to rule, and a steady flow of taxes.

The Ottomans found loyal servants through the devshirme. They took Christian boys from conquered lands, converted them to Islam and trained them as Janissaries or government officials. Because these men had no ties to local noble families, they were loyal to the sultan alone.

For revenue, the Ottomans used tax farming: the government sold or granted the right to collect taxes in a region to private individuals, who kept part of what they collected. The Mughals relied on zamindars, landholding elites who collected taxes from peasants and sent a share to the central government. In both empires, the people who actually gathered the taxes were not the central government's own officials.

g2b.title: Orders to the great lords
g2b.attr: Practice passage in the voice of a Tokugawa official in Japan, after 1603.
g2b.label: Practice passage written only from your teacher's Unit 3 study guide; not a real quotation.
paras: By order of the shogun, each regional lord shall live in the capital every other year. In this way no lord may stay long in his own domain, gathering strength, without the shogun's knowledge.
The samurai shall no longer serve only as warriors. They shall become officials who receive a salary and carry out the business of government.

Contact with foreigners shall be sharply limited, and the Christian religion is banned throughout the land. These rules shall keep the peace that the shogun has brought after long years of war among the lords.

g2c.title: Kings, tsars and emperors
g2c.attr: Practice passage written in the style of a modern historian.
g2c.label: Practice passage written only from your teacher's Unit 3 study guide; not a real quotation.
paras: Rulers in many regions faced the same problem: powerful nobles and officials who might act on their own. Louis XIV of France, the classic example of absolutism, made the great nobles live at his palace of Versailles, where he could watch them and keep them dependent on him.

Peter the Great took a different path in Russia. He westernized the country by modernizing the military and building St. Petersburg, and his Table of Ranks promoted officials by service rather than by birth. In China, the Qing kept the Confucian civil service exam and shared government posts between Manchu and Han officials to win acceptance.

Rulers also displayed their power. Grand buildings such as the Taj Mahal, Versailles and the Temple of the Sun in Cuzco showed off their wealth, while religion justified their rule: European kings claimed divine right, the Mexica used human sacrifice, and Songhai rulers promoted Islam.

g3a.label: Practice passage written only from your teacher's Unit 3 study guide; not a real quotation.
paras: In 1517 a monk named Martin Luther posted his Ninety-Five Theses, challenging the authority of the Catholic Church. We had always been taught that the Church spoke for all Christians, and few had dared to question it.

Now new Protestant churches have formed in many towns. Some of my neighbors follow Luther, while others remain loyal to Rome, and the two sides no longer pray together. Western Europe, which once shared one Church, is divided.

g3b.title: The Catholic response
g3b.attr: Practice passage written in the style of a modern historian.
g3b.label: Practice passage written only from your teacher's Unit 3 study guide; not a real quotation.
paras: The Catholic Church did not simply accept the Protestant challenge. It answered with reforms of its own, known as the Catholic or Counter Reformation. At the Council of Trent, Church leaders reaffirmed Catholic teachings and addressed corruption within the Church.

A new Catholic order, the Jesuits, spread the faith through missionaries and schools, carrying Catholicism far beyond Europe. Taken together, the two Reformations spread Christianity more widely and made it more diverse than it had been before.
The divisions also led to violence. The Thirty Years' War (1618–1648), one of the major wars of European history, was fought partly over Protestant and Catholic identity.

g3c.title: Sunni and Shi'a
g3c.attr: Practice passage written in the style of a modern historian.
g3c.label: Practice passage written only from your teacher's Unit 3 study guide; not a real quotation.
paras: The split between Sunni and Shi'a Muslims was centuries old by 1450, but the rise of two rival empires gave it new force. The Ottomans were Sunni, and the Safavids were Shi'a.

As the two empires fought over land, their political rivalry deepened the religious divide. Each state used religious identity as a weapon in its conflict with the other, so that a war over territory became a struggle between two forms of Islam.
The result was a lasting religious border in Southwest Asia, drawn as much by politics as by belief.

g3d.title: New faiths from old
g3d.attr: Practice passage written in the style of a modern historian of South Asia.
g3d.label: Practice passage written only from your teacher's Unit 3 study guide; not a real quotation.

A century later the Mughal emperor Akbar went further in blending traditions. His Din-i-Ilahi mixed elements of Islam, Hinduism and other faiths. Historians call this kind of mixing of religious traditions syncretism.
Both developments show that contact between religions in this period produced new beliefs, not only conflict.

g4a.title: Same tools, different forms
g4a.attr: Practice passage written in the style of a modern historian.
g4a.label: Practice passage written only from your teacher's Unit 3 study guide; not a real quotation.
paras: The land-based empires of this period used many of the same tools, but in different ways. All of them relied on gunpowder and professional armies. The Ottomans organized the Janissaries, the Qing relied on the banner system, and Russia sent Cossacks across the steppe.

Every empire also needed to explain why its rulers deserved to rule, and most turned to religion and grand buildings. European kings claimed divine right, Chinese emperors claimed the Mandate of Heaven, and Ottoman sultans claimed to be caliphs.

The point of comparing them is not to list these facts but to explain them: similar problems led empires to similar tools, while their different histories and religions shaped the form each tool took.

g4b.title: Tolerance and its limits
g4b.attr: Practice passage written in the style of a modern historian.
g4b.label: Practice passage written only from your teacher's Unit 3 study guide; not a real quotation.
paras: Empires in this period took very different approaches to the religions of their subjects. The Mughal emperor Akbar practiced religious tolerance and abolished the jizya, the tax on non-Muslims. The Safavids, by contrast, imposed Shi'a Islam as the state religion, and European rulers fought wars over Protestant and Catholic identity.
The Mughal Empire offers a comparison within a single state. Akbar's successor Aurangzeb brought back the jizya and enforced stricter Sunni rule. His policies fueled rebellions across the empire.
The contrast between the two emperors suggests that religious policy could strengthen or weaken an empire as much as its armies could.

Every empire also needed money. The Ottomans used tax farming, the Mughals relied on zamindars, and the Mexica and Inca collected tribute. The methods differed, but each pulled wealth from subjects to fund the empire.

sections.name: SAQs
tips: Use TEA for every part: T = Topic sentence (answer the question directly, restating its words), E = Evidence (a specific person, place, term or date), A = Analysis (explain how the evidence proves your point, using "which led to," "because" or "this allowed").
Label your answers A, B and C and write in complete sentences. No introduction or thesis.
"Identify" or "describe" means give accurate details. "Explain" means show how or why.
Stay inside 1450 to 1750 unless the question says otherwise.
Aim for about 13 minutes per SAQ: about 1 to plan and 12 to write.
Self-check: Did I give a specific example? Did I explain the connection? Right empire, right century?

P7.title: A historian on Chaldiran
P7.attr: Argument based on your 3.1 slides, Pocket Dictionary and AMSCO.
P7.label: Practice source (written for practice from your class materials; not a verbatim quotation).
P7.text: At Chaldiran in 1514, Ottoman cannons and Janissary musketeers cut down the Safavid cavalry. The defeat halted Safavid expansion to the west, and the Safavids spent the next century rebuilding their army with firearms. Yet the battle was never only about weapons or borders. The Sunni Ottomans and the Shi'a Safavids each regarded the other's Islam as a betrayal of the faith, and the war turned that religious divide into a frontier between two states.

P9.title: Settling Europe's religious wars
P9.label: Practice source (written for practice from your class materials; not a verbatim quotation).
P9.text: In 1555 the Peace of Augsburg allowed each German prince to decide whether his state would be Catholic or Lutheran; subjects who disagreed could move. Nearly a century later, after the Thirty Years' War had brought famine and disease to much of Central Europe, the Peace of Westphalia (1648) added Calvinism as a third choice. Afterward France, Spain and Italy were mostly Catholic, northern Europe was Lutheran or Calvinist, and England had its own Protestant state church.

In 1517 Martin Luther attacked the sale of indulgences in his Ninety-Five Theses, and German princes backed him to escape the Pope's power.

sections.name: Mock MCQs
examTips: Treat this like the real test: turn the Timer on, leave Shuffle off, and do all 13 questions without looking anything up.
Aim for about one minute per question. Flag hard ones and come back.
When you finish, do the Mock SAQs tab (choose 2 of the 3, about 13 minutes each), then use Retest Missed Questions.
tips: Read the attribution line first: who wrote it, when, and why. A Tokugawa decree, an ambassador and a modern historian each have a different purpose.
Find the main idea of each paragraph before you look at the choices. Many questions ask about one paragraph only.

For "best used as evidence of" or "best illustrates" questions, first name the bigger development the source shows (gunpowder expansion, loyal elites, legitimacy, revenue, religious change), then pick the choice that matches it.
The wrong choices are usually true-but-not-in-the-source, from the wrong empire or century, or too extreme. Cross them out with the X button.
"Practice passage" sources were written for this kit from your class materials. They are not real quotations, so don't quote them on the test.

M1.title: At the sultan's court
M1.attr: Practice passage in the voice of a European ambassador at the court of Suleiman the Magnificent, mid-1500s.
M1.label: Practice passage written from your class materials (textbook, study guide, slides); not a real quotation.
paras: In all that great assembly, no man owed his rank to anything but his own merit and the will of the sultan. There was no distinction attached to birth. The sultan himself chooses his ministers and officials, and he looks at their ability, not their family or wealth. Many of the men who now hold the highest offices were born the sons of shepherds and herdsmen and were taken into the sultan's service as boys.
Among us in Europe it is very different. A man's birth decides everything, and offices and commands go to those of noble family whether or not they deserve them.

This is why the Turks succeed in all that they attempt and are a ruling race, while we in our countries quarrel among ourselves. If we do not change, I fear for what will come when their armies, with their great guns and disciplined infantry, march against us again.

M2.title: Two emperors, one empire
M2.attr: Practice passage written in the style of a modern historian of Mughal India.
M2.label: Practice passage written from your class materials (textbook, study guide, slides); not a real quotation.
paras: Akbar understood that a Muslim dynasty could not rule India's Hindu majority by force alone. He abolished the jizya, the tax on non-Muslims, married Hindu wives, and gave Hindu nobles high posts in his government. He even sponsored a blended faith, the Din-i Ilahi, though it attracted few followers. During his long reign the empire expanded across northern India while keeping the loyalty of many Hindu nobles.

His great-grandson Aurangzeb took a different course. He pushed the empire to its largest size, but he restored the jizya, enforced strict Sunni practice and opposed Hindu influences at court. In the Deccan, Hindu Maratha fighters led by Shivaji waged a long guerrilla war against him, and other groups rose in revolt.

The contrast suggests that the empire's strength depended less on the size of its armies than on the cooperation of its diverse subjects. When that cooperation was withdrawn, even the largest Mughal army could not hold the empire together.

M3.title: Rivals of the faith
M3.attr: Practice passage written in the style of a modern historian of the Middle East.
M3.label: Practice passage written from your class materials (textbook, study guide, slides); not a real quotation.
paras: When Ismail I founded the Safavid state in 1501, he made Shi'a Islam its official religion and required his Sunni subjects to convert. To the Sunni Ottomans next door, this was both a religious challenge and a political threat, since Shi'a sympathizers lived inside Ottoman Anatolia.

The two empires met at Chaldiran in 1514. The Safavid cavalry was famous for its courage, but Ottoman artillery and Janissary musketeers cut it down. The Ottomans followed their victory with an embargo against Safavid silk merchants, trying to starve the shah's treasury of trade.

For more than a century the frontier between the empires remained a line between Sunni and Shi'a lands, marked by places such as Tabriz, where the Ottomans stopped Safavid forces in 1541. Only after the Safavids rebuilt their army with firearms under Shah Abbas I, and after religious fervor had faded at court, did the two states conclude a lasting peace in 1639.

M4.title: Paris and the Huguenots
M4.attr: Practice passage in the voice of a French Protestant (Huguenot) looking back from the late 1680s. The words of Henry IV are as quoted in your textbook (AMSCO 3.3).
M4.label: Practice passage written from your class materials (textbook, study guide, slides); not a real quotation.
paras: Our fathers fought long wars for the right to worship as Calvin taught, and France was torn apart by them. Henry of Navarre, raised in our faith, became king only by taking the Catholic Mass in 1593. "Paris is well worth a Mass," he is reported to have said. Some of us called him a traitor, but in 1598 he gave us the Edict of Nantes, and for the first time we could worship openly in our towns.

Now King Louis has revoked the edict. Our churches are torn down, our pastors are banished, and our children must be raised Catholic. Weavers, goldsmiths and merchants are leaving for Holland, England and the German lands, taking their skills with them, and France is poorer for it.

M5.title: Gold, salt and guns
M5.attr: Practice passage written in the style of a modern historian of West Africa.
M5.label: Practice passage written from your class materials (textbook, study guide, slides); not a real quotation.
paras: By the late 1400s, Songhai controlled the great cities of the middle Niger, Gao and Timbuktu, and the caravan trade that carried West African gold north across the Sahara in exchange for salt. Sunni Ali had built this state in the 1460s and 1470s, using swift cavalry and control of the Niger River to conquer Timbuktu and Jenne. His successors, especially Askia the Great, made Islam the official religion and staffed their government with scholars trained in the madrasas of Timbuktu.

That wealth drew the attention of Morocco. In 1591 a Moroccan army crossed the desert carrying firearms, still rare south of the Sahara. At Tondibi, near Gao, it defeated a much larger Songhai army that had no such weapons. Morocco had come for the gold routes, and with this victory Songhai's control of them was broken.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the ambassador's main claim in the first paragraph?
options: Ottoman officials rose by ability, not birth
Ottoman officials were chosen from the empire's wealthiest noble families
The sultan allowed his officials to elect his ministers
The sons of shepherds were barred from the sultan's service
questions.exp: "No man owed his rank to anything but his own merit and the will of the sultan."
why: He says the opposite: birth brings no distinction.
He says the sultan himself chooses them.
He says many high officials were shepherds' sons.

questions.stem: The pattern the ambassador describes was made possible most directly by
options: the devshirme, which recruited boys regardless of family
the Ottoman adoption of the Confucian civil service examination
the Ottoman practice of tax farming, which sold the right to collect taxes
the millet system, which let each religious group run its own affairs
questions.exp: Boys "taken into the sultan's service" = the devshirme.
why: The exams were Chinese.
Tax farming was about revenue, not choosing officials.
The millet system was about religious communities, not recruitment.

questions.stem: The ambassador's comparison in the second and third paragraphs is most likely intended to
options: persuade the sultan to adopt European customs of inheritance
show that European armies were stronger than Ottoman armies
warn Europeans that rank by birth left them weaker
argue that the Ottomans would soon decline because of their system
questions.exp: He contrasts Ottoman merit with European birth and fears what Ottoman armies will do next.

He fears the Ottoman armies.
He says their system is why they succeed.

questions.stem: Which of the following best states the historian's argument?
options: Aurangzeb's larger army made the empire more stable than it had been under Akbar
Akbar's Din-i Ilahi converted most of India to a new religion
Religious policy had little effect on the stability of the Mughal Empire
Mughal power rested on subjects' cooperation more than on armies
questions.exp: Final paragraph: strength depended on cooperation, not army size.
why: The historian says the largest army could not hold the empire together.
The passage says it attracted few followers.
The whole passage links religious policy to peace or revolt.

questions.stem: According to the passage, which most directly contributed to the rebellions described in the second paragraph?
options: Akbar's decision to give Hindu nobles high positions in government
The popularity of the Din-i Ilahi among Hindu nobles
A Safavid invasion that drew the Mughal army out of the Deccan
Aurangzeb's return of the jizya and strict Sunni rule
questions.exp: Aurangzeb restored the jizya and enforced strict Sunni rule; the Marathas and others revolted.
why: That built cooperation; the revolts came under Aurangzeb.
It attracted few followers.
The passage mentions no Safavid invasion.

questions.stem: Akbar's approach in the first paragraph is most similar to which of the following?
options: Ismail I's demand that Sunnis in Persia convert to Shi'a Islam
Louis XIV's revocation of the Edict of Nantes
The Ottoman millet system for religious communities
The Tokugawa ban on Christianity in Japan
questions.exp: Both accepted religious diversity to keep a large empire stable.
why: That is forced conformity, closer to Aurangzeb.
That ended toleration.
That is restriction, not tolerance.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the Ottomans saw the Safavid state as a threat mainly because
options: the Safavids had a stronger navy that threatened Ottoman ports
its Shi'a identity was both a religious and a political threat
the Safavids had allied with European Christians against the sultan
the Safavids controlled Mecca and Medina
questions.exp: Paragraph 1: a religious challenge and a political threat, since Shi'a sympathizers lived in Anatolia.
why: The Safavids had no significant navy, and the passage never mentions one.
No alliance is mentioned.
The holy cities were under Ottoman, not Safavid, protection.

questions.stem: The second paragraph can best be used as evidence that
options: gunpowder weapons could defeat famous cavalry armies
religious belief decided the outcome of battles in this period
the Safavids were the stronger military power in 1514
trade had no role in the conflict between the two empires
questions.exp: Artillery and Janissary muskets cut down the famous Safavid cavalry.
why: The paragraph credits artillery and muskets.
They lost at Chaldiran.
The Ottomans used a silk embargo as a weapon.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the change the historian identifies in the final paragraph?
options: Religious fervor faded and a lasting peace followed
A shift from peaceful trade to constant warfare after 1639
The Ottoman conversion to Shi'a Islam, which ended the conflict
The Safavid conquest of Istanbul under Shah Abbas I
questions.exp: Religious fervor faded at court, and a lasting peace came in 1639.
why: The order is reversed: war first, peace in 1639.
The Ottomans remained Sunni.
There was no such conquest.

questions.stem: The author's description of Henry IV in the first paragraph suggests that Henry
options: was a devout Catholic from birth who wanted to destroy the Huguenots completely
refused to change his religion even to become king
was forced out of France by the Catholic nobility
valued peace and the throne over one faith, then protected Protestants
questions.exp: "Paris is well worth a Mass": he converted to win the throne, then protected the Huguenots in 1598.
why: He was raised Protestant and gave them the Edict of Nantes.
He took the Mass in 1593.
He became king and issued the edict.

questions.stem: The second paragraph can best be used as evidence that the revocation of the Edict of Nantes
options: ended religious conflict in France by uniting all French people in one faith
weakened France economically by driving skilled Protestant workers abroad
strengthened the Huguenot churches by forcing them to organize
was a response to a Huguenot attempt to seize the French throne

Their churches were torn down and pastors banished.

options: The European takeover of the trans-Saharan gold trade
Gunpowder driving state expansion beyond Eurasia
The spread of Shi'a Islam from Persia into West Africa
The success of cavalry armies against early firearms

why: The invaders were Moroccan, not European.
The passage mentions no Shi'a influence.

English monarchs whose power was limited by the Bill of Rights
Ottoman sultans who claimed to be caliph and used trained officials
Russian tsars who expanded by hiring Cossacks to fight in Siberia

sections.name: Mock SAQs
examTips: Like the real test: choose TWO of the three SAQs. Turn the Timer on and give yourself about 13 minutes each.
Write complete sentences for A, B and C, and only then check your answers.
tips: Use TEA for every part: T = Topic sentence (answer the question directly, restating its words), E = Evidence (a specific person, place, term or date), A = Analysis (explain how the evidence proves your point, using "which led to," "because" or "this allowed").
Label your answers A, B and C and write in complete sentences. No introduction or thesis.
"Identify" or "describe" means give accurate details. "Explain" means show how or why.
Stay inside 1450 to 1750 unless the question says otherwise.
Aim for about 13 minutes per SAQ: about 1 to plan and 12 to write.
Self-check: Did I give a specific example? Did I explain the connection? Right empire, right century?

R5.title: The oath of an English justice of the peace
R5.attr: Oath of office under the Tudor monarchs, as quoted in AMSCO Topic 3.2.
R5.text: [You shall] swear that as Justices of the Peace . . . in all articles in the King's Commission to you directed, ye shall do equal right to the poor and to the rich after your cunning wit, and power, and after the laws and customs of the realm and statutes thereof made.

P6.title: The teachings of Guru Nanak
P6.attr: Summary based on your 3.3 slides and AMSCO Topic 3.3.
P6.label: Practice source (written for practice from your class materials; not a verbatim quotation).
P6.text: Guru Nanak, who lived in the Punjab in the late 1400s, taught that there is one God, who can be reached through personal devotion, meditation and honest living rather than through ritual. He welcomed followers from Hindu and Muslim families alike and rejected the caste system, teaching that all people are equal before God.

parts.prompt: Describe one duty of a justice of the peace, according to the excerpt.
parts.skill: Describing a claim from a source
parts.model: One duty was to give equal justice to all people. The oath says justices must 'do equal right to the poor and to the rich' according to 'the laws and customs of the realm.' This shows they enforced the monarch's law fairly in the counties.
tea: One duty was to give equal justice to all people.
The oath says justices must 'do equal right to the poor and to the rich' according to 'the laws and customs of the realm.'
This shows they enforced the monarch's law fairly in the counties.
parts.earns: You describe enforcing the king's law, treating rich and poor equally, or carrying out the King's Commission.
parts.weak: "They were officials." Describe what they had to do.

parts.prompt: Explain how officials like those in the excerpt helped English monarchs centralize power.
parts.model: Justices of the peace helped centralize power by carrying the monarch's authority into every county. Under the Tudors (1485–1603) their numbers and responsibilities grew, while feudal lords lost power. Because local order now depended on officials enforcing royal law, the crown no longer needed to rely on independent nobles.
tea: Justices of the peace helped centralize power by carrying the monarch's authority into every county.
Under the Tudors (1485–1603) their numbers and responsibilities grew, while feudal lords lost power.
Because local order now depended on officials enforcing royal law, the crown no longer needed to rely on independent nobles.
parts.earns: You connect the justices to weaker nobles or stronger royal control with a specific detail.
parts.weak: Repeating part A.

parts.prompt: Explain one difference between how England and France were governed by about 1700.
parts.model: England developed a limited monarchy while France became an absolute monarchy. In England the Bill of Rights of 1689 required Parliament's agreement for taxes and an army, while Louis XIV of France ruled by divine right and said, 'I am the state.' So English kings were checked by Parliament, while the French king held complete authority.
tea: England developed a limited monarchy while France became an absolute monarchy.
In England the Bill of Rights of 1689 required Parliament's agreement for taxes and an army, while Louis XIV of France ruled by divine right and said, 'I am the state.'
So English kings were checked by Parliament, while the French king held complete authority.
parts.earns: England (Parliament, Bill of Rights) versus France (absolutism, Louis XIV, intendants, Versailles), with an explanation.
parts.weak: Describing only France.

parts.prompt: Identify one way gunpowder helped a land-based empire expand between 1450 and 1750.
parts.model: Gunpowder helped the Ottoman Empire take fortified cities. In 1453 Mehmed II's huge bronze cannons broke the walls of Constantinople. Taking the city ended the Byzantine Empire and gave the Ottomans a capital that controlled the Bosporus.
tea: Gunpowder helped the Ottoman Empire take fortified cities.
In 1453 Mehmed II's huge bronze cannons broke the walls of Constantinople.
Taking the city ended the Byzantine Empire and gave the Ottomans a capital that controlled the Bosporus.
parts.earns: Any accurate example: Constantinople, Chaldiran, Panipat, Tondibi, Cossacks in Siberia, Manchu banners.
parts.weak: "They had guns." Name the empire and the event.

parts.prompt: Explain one similarity in how two empires expanded in this period.
parts.model: The Mughals and Morocco both used firearms to defeat larger armies. Babur's cannons and matchlocks won at Panipat in 1526, and Moroccan musketeers beat a bigger Songhai army at Tondibi in 1591. In both cases gunpowder gave smaller forces an advantage over armies using older tactics, which let them take new territory.
tea: The Mughals and Morocco both used firearms to defeat larger armies.
Babur's cannons and matchlocks won at Panipat in 1526, and Moroccan musketeers beat a bigger Songhai army at Tondibi in 1591.
In both cases gunpowder gave smaller forces an advantage over armies using older tactics, which let them take new territory.
parts.earns: Two empires, one shared method, and why it worked.
parts.weak: Two separate descriptions with no comparison.

parts.prompt: Explain one reason a land-based empire declined by the 1700s.
parts.model: One reason was the cost of maintaining large armies. Aurangzeb's long wars in the Deccan against the Marathas drained the Mughal treasury. Without money and with revolts spreading, the empire weakened, letting Britain and France gain power in India.
tea: One reason was the cost of maintaining large armies.
Aurangzeb's long wars in the Deccan against the Marathas drained the Mughal treasury.
Without money and with revolts spreading, the empire weakened, letting Britain and France gain power in India.
parts.earns: A specific cause (costly wars, weak heirs and harem politics, failure to modernize, high taxes, rebellions) for a named empire.
parts.weak: "It got weak." Explain why.

parts.prompt: Describe one teaching of Guru Nanak, according to the passage.
parts.skill: Describing a claim from a source
parts.model: One teaching was that all people are equal before God. The passage says Nanak 'rejected the caste system.' This challenged the Hindu social order that ranked people by birth.
tea: One teaching was that all people are equal before God.
The passage says Nanak 'rejected the caste system.'
This challenged the Hindu social order that ranked people by birth.
parts.earns: One God, devotion over ritual, equality, rejecting caste, welcoming Hindus and Muslims.
parts.weak: "He taught about God." Be specific.

parts.prompt: Explain how the development of Sikhism shows interaction between belief systems.
parts.model: Sikhism shows interaction because it grew out of contact between Hindus and Muslims in the Punjab. It combined devotion to one God, similar to Islam, with ideas of personal devotion found in Hinduism, and welcomed followers from both. This makes it an example of syncretism, a new faith created by contact between existing ones.
tea: Sikhism shows interaction because it grew out of contact between Hindus and Muslims in the Punjab.
It combined devotion to one God, similar to Islam, with ideas of personal devotion found in Hinduism, and welcomed followers from both.
This makes it an example of syncretism, a new faith created by contact between existing ones.
parts.earns: Hindu–Muslim contact, syncretism, and how the faith reflects both.
parts.weak: Calling it a mix with no explanation.

parts.prompt: Explain one way Mughal rulers' treatment of the Sikhs changed between 1550 and 1700.
parts.model: Mughal treatment of the Sikhs changed from support to persecution. Akbar gave land grants to the Sikhs, but in 1606 Jahangir had Guru Arjan executed. This persecution pushed Sikhs toward armed self-defense, and in 1699 Guru Gobind Singh founded the Khalsa.
tea: Mughal treatment of the Sikhs changed from support to persecution.
Akbar gave land grants to the Sikhs, but in 1606 Jahangir had Guru Arjan executed.
This persecution pushed Sikhs toward armed self-defense, and in 1699 Guru Gobind Singh founded the Khalsa.
parts.earns: A specific before and after, with an explanation.
parts.weak: Describing only Akbar or only Jahangir.
